lessons.title: Why and how a tractor is split
lessons.html:
What does splitting a tractor mean?

Most tractors have no full chassis. The engine, the clutch housing, the gearbox and the back axle are bolted together and they are the frame. To reach the clutch or the front of the gearbox, you must separate the tractor into two halves. This is called splitting the tractor.

You split a tractor to:

  • replace a worn or slipping clutch;
  • replace the rear main oil seal of the engine;
  • repair the gearbox input shaft or the flywheel;
  • reach other parts between the engine and the gearbox.

This is a dangerous job

When the tractor is split, each half can fall over or roll. The engine half alone can weigh well over a tonne. People have been crushed doing this job. You must work with your supervisor or a trained mechanic.

  • Use a proper splitting stand or a set of strong stands and wedges made for the job.
  • Use a hoist or crane rated for the weight.
  • Never use bricks, wooden crates or a single jack to hold a tractor half.
  • Never put any part of your body between the two halves while they move.
  • Keep other people away from the work area.

Planning

  1. Read the workshop manual. It shows where to split and the special stands needed.
  2. Get the new clutch, seals, gaskets and bolts ready.
  3. Choose a flat, hard concrete floor with space to roll the halves apart.

lessons.title: Separating the two halves
lessons.html:
Before you split

  1. Park on level concrete, switch off and remove the key.
  2. Disconnect and remove the battery.
  3. Drain the fluids the manual lists, such as transmission oil. Catch them in clean trays.
  4. Remove the bonnet, side panels and anything in the way, such as the fuel tank on some models.
  5. Disconnect all links between the two halves: wiring loom, throttle cable, fuel pipes, hydraulic pipes, steering pipes, clutch linkage, drive shaft to the front axle. Tag each one and take photos.
  6. Cap all hydraulic and fuel pipes.

Supporting the halves

  • Put wedges between the front axle and the engine so the front cannot rock on its pivot.
  • Support the engine half on a splitting stand or hoist.
  • Support the gearbox half on stands and chock the back wheels.

Splitting

  1. Remove the bolts between the engine and the clutch housing, leaving two bolts for last.
  2. Fit two long guide studs in place of bolts, if the manual says so. They keep the halves lined up.
  3. Remove the last bolts.
  4. Slowly roll or slide one half straight away from the other. Keep both halves level. Watch that no pipe or wire is still connected.
  5. Check both halves are stable before you start other work.

lessons.title: Joining the tractor and checking
lessons.html:
Getting ready to join

Do the repair work, for example fitting the new clutch, as the manual says. Before joining:

  • Clean the faces of both housings and fit a new gasket or sealant as the manual says.
  • Line up the clutch plate with a clutch alignment tool so the gearbox shaft will go in.
  • Put a light film of the correct grease on the input shaft splines if the manual says so.
  • Check that nothing has been left inside the housing.

Joining

  1. Put the gearbox in gear so you can turn the input shaft by turning a back wheel. This helps line up the splines.
  2. Fit the guide studs.
  3. Slowly bring the halves together, keeping them level and straight.
  4. Never pull the halves together with the bolts. If they do not meet, move them apart and check the alignment.
  5. Fit the bolts and tighten them evenly to the manual torque.
  6. Remove the front axle wedges.

Reconnecting and testing

  • Reconnect all pipes, wires and links using your tags and photos.
  • Refill fluids to the right levels.
  • Fit the battery, start the tractor and check for leaks.
  • Check the clutch free play and that all gears select.
  • Check steering, brakes and hydraulics work before any test drive.

Key points

  • Splitting a tractor is dangerous; work with a trained mechanic.
  • Use proper splitting stands and lifting gear, never bricks or one jack.
  • Wedge the front axle so the engine half cannot rock.
  • Tag and cap every disconnected pipe and wire.
  • Never pull the halves together with the bolts.
